analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal extraction $10 per ton to fund mitigation of coal-train dust and noise along rail routes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a $10-per-ton tax on coal extracted in the United States and deposit the money into a new Coal Mitigation Trust Fund. States that ship at least 2.5 million tons of coal by rail a year could draw on the fund to deal with the noise, dust, traffic, pollution, and emergencies that heavy coal train traffic brings, and to help coal workers adjust to job losses. It would also require the Transportation Department to write rules requiring coal rail cars to be covered so coal dust cannot escape, and it would give coal export port property a 50-year depreciation period, a tax break that lowers the cost of building coal export terminals.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along the rail lines that carry millions of tons of coal, in states from the Powder River Basin routes in the West to ports in the East, would get a dedicated funding stream for mitigating noise, vibration, traffic delays, pollution, and emergencies tied to coal trains. Coal workers facing layoffs would be eligible for worker adjustment assistance. Communities' exposure to coal dust would fall because railroads would have to cover coal cars or use equivalent technology.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $10-per-ton excise tax on coal extracted in the United States, effective after enactment.
Creates a Coal Mitigation Trust Fund in the Treasury and automatically credits all receipts of the new coal excise tax to it.

Allows the fund to pay states, on a population-based formula, for mitigating noise, vibration, traffic delays, pollution and other threats to public health, and emergencies connected with coal transported by rail, and for related worker adjustment assistance; states qualify only if at least 2.5 million tons of coal per year moves through them by rail.

Directs the Secretary of Transportation to issue regulations requiring all coal rail cars to be covered, or to incorporate suitable alternative technology, so that coal and coal dust do not escape during transport.
Bars trust fund money from being used to pay for any expense a coal producer or transporter is already legally required to provide.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies pay the $10-per-ton tax, which would likely be passed through into the price of coal and ultimately to utilities and electricity customers who burn it. The 50-year depreciation period for coal export port property reduces federal tax revenue, and the coal industry and export terminal developers bear the cost of covering rail cars. Railroads transporting coal would need to cover cars or adopt dust-control technology.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal producers, railroads, and electricity customers

drawbacks.text: The excise tax on coal extraction would raise the cost of coal, a cost that coal producers would likely pass on to power plants and ultimately to households and businesses that buy electricity generated from coal.

The bill extends the depreciation period for coal export port property to 50 years, a tax treatment that lowers the after-tax cost of building new coal export terminals; this provision cuts federal revenue and encourages export infrastructure even as the tax penalizes extraction.

Mitigation money reaches only the 50 states that ship at least 2.5 million tons of coal by rail per year, leaving communities in states with lighter coal train traffic to absorb the same noise, dust, and safety burdens without fund support.
Trust fund spending is available only as provided in annual appropriations acts, so Congress could decline to appropriate the money even after the tax is collected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design follows a polluter-pays logic: the industry whose product generates the dust, noise, and traffic pays a tax that funds relief for the communities along the routes, and a mandate to cover coal cars attacks the dust problem at its source. The main offsetting weakness is the 50-year depreciation break for coal export port property, which reduces federal revenue and subsidizes new export terminals, pulling in the opposite direction from the tax. The overall benefit to corridor communities is real but depends on annual appropriations, and some of the tax's cost would reach electricity customers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2013 and referred to two House committees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on June 17, 2013.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction.

The following day, June 18, 2013, it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or consideration in the Senate during the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers and companies building coal export terminals avoided a $10-per-ton tax and a federal mandate to cover coal cars, and railroads kept operating uncovered coal cars through rail corridor communities. Residents along coal routes got no dedicated mitigation funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal producers and export terminal developers

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 17, 2013 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral with jurisdiction over the excise tax
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 17, 2013 and took no action on it for the remainder of the 113th Congress.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral with jurisdiction over the rail car mandate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to its Railroads Subcommittee on June 18, 2013, and took no further action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Republican-controlled committees did not act.

industries.note: A $10-per-ton tax on every ton of coal extracted in the United States would directly raise their cost of production, and covering coal cars adds expense; the industry's interest in avoiding the tax ran against communities that bear the dust and noise of coal transport.

industries.industry: Coal export terminal developers and port operators
industries.note: The bill would let them depreciate coal port property over 50 years, reducing the after-tax cost of building export terminals with capacity above 1 million tons a year, even as the bill taxes extraction; its interest ran alongside the export industry, not the corridor communities the tax was meant to help.

Railroads would face the cost of covering coal cars or adopting dust-control technology, a direct burden; on the other hand, the extended depreciation on port property and the longer recovery period for railroad grading and tunnel bores reduce their tax burden.

industries.industry: Coal-exporting states and rail corridor communities
industries.note: States shipping at least 2.5 million tons of coal by rail a year would gain access to the mitigation trust fund for noise, pollution, and safety problems, and eligible coal workers would gain access to adjustment assistance.
